etymology: From the Old French potage, that which is put into the pot; hence a thick boiled dish of pulse or herbs, the plainest hot food of the poor man’s kitchen — and the price at which a birthright was once sold.
biblical_def: Pottage is a thick boiled mess of lentiles, beans, or herbs, seethed in the common pot — the cheapest hot dish the ancient kitchen could set down. Its fame in Scripture is not culinary but moral. Jacob sod pottage; Esau came in from the field faint, saw the red mess steaming, and cried, “Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage; for I am faint” (Gen 25:30). Jacob named his price, and Esau sold his birthright — the double portion, the headship of the house, and the covenant line running down from Abraham toward Christ — for one hot dinner. The Holy Ghost records the transaction with a merciless plainness: “he did eat and drink, and rose up, and went his way: thus Esau despised his birthright” (Gen 25:34). He did not agonize over it; he ate and walked off. Hebrews fixes the verdict for the church: he was a profane person, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright, and afterward found no place of repentance though he sought it carefully with tears (Heb 12:16-17). The word appears again on Elisha’s table at Gilgal, where a great pot of pottage was poisoned by wild gourds gathered in ignorance, and the sons of the prophets cried, “there is death in the pot” (2Ki 4:40) — until the prophet cast in meal and healed it, a small parable of the word of God sweetening a poisoned inheritance.
webster_summary: A thick boiled dish of pulse or herbs; proverbially, the trifling price for which Esau sold his birthright.
webster_full: POTTAGE, a species of food composed of meat, pulse, or herbs boiled together and softened by heat; broth; soup.
From the French potage, from pot, the vessel in which it is seethed.
The pottage of lentiles for which Esau sold his birthright (Gen 25:34).
A common dish of the poor, and of the schools of the prophets (2Ki 4:38).
Proverbially, any small and present gratification bought at a ruinous price.
scriptures: And Jacob sod pottage: and Esau came from the field, and he was faint:
And Esau said to Jacob, Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage; for I am faint: therefore was his name called Edom.
Then Jacob gave Esau bread and pottage of lentiles; and he did eat and drink, and rose up, and went his way: thus Esau despised his birthright.

So they poured out for the men to eat. And it came to pass, as they were eating of the pottage, that they cried out, and said, O thou man of God, there is death in the pot. And they could not eat thereof.
corruption_summary: Esau’s bargain is retold as a sympathetic hunger story rather than as profanity — and the appetite-driven trade of covenant privilege for present comfort goes on unnamed.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the softening of Esau. He is pitied: he was faint, he had been in the field, he thought he was at the point to die, and the birthright was only a legal abstraction anyway — while Jacob was the schemer who took advantage of a starving brother. Scripture will not have it. Jacob’s dealing is nowhere commended, but the inspired verdict falls on Esau alone and it is one word: despised. He was not dying; he rose up and went his way. What he did was to weigh the covenant of God against a bowl of lentiles and judge the lentiles worth more, because the lentiles were hot and now and the covenant was distant and promised. Hebrews therefore calls him a profane person — not a scandalous sinner but a secular one, a man for whom nothing was holy because nothing unseen was real. That is the sin the modern heart commits daily and refuses to name: the marriage traded for an appetite, the Lord’s day traded for a livelihood, the child’s catechism traded for the travel league, the conscience traded for the promotion. Every one of them is Esau’s arithmetic, and every one of them looks reasonable while the pot is still steaming.

Recover the birthright’s worth by looking at what came after. Esau got his dinner and kept it about an hour; he lost a place in the line that ran to Bethlehem. And when he came at last, with a great and exceeding bitter cry, to seek the blessing, he found no place of repentance though he sought it carefully with tears (Heb 12:17) — the tears of a man who wanted the loss reversed, not the sin forgiven. Let the believer read his own bargains by that light. Nothing sold for pottage is ever sold at the price the seller thought. Set against it the mercy of the pot at Gilgal: there was death in the dish, and the man of God cast in meal, and there was no harm in the pot (2Ki 4:41). What Esau despised, Christ purchased and gives freely to those born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh, but of God — and He is the meal cast into an inheritance we had already poisoned.
roots_summary: A boiled dish of pulse; the byword for a trifling present gain bought with an eternal loss.
roots_lines: Pottage — Old French potage, from pot; that which is boiled in the pot.
Hebrew nazid, a boiled dish, from zid, to seethe or boil up (Gen 25:29; 2Ki 4:38).
The pottage of Gen 25 was of lentiles, and red — whence Esau’s name Edom.
Heb 12:16 renders the price “one morsel of meat” and names Esau profane.
At Gilgal the pottage was death until healed by meal cast in (2Ki 4:40-41).
usage: Esau did not agonize over the sale — he ate, rose up, and went his way.
The birthright was covenant, headship, and double portion; the price was one hot dish.
There is death in the pot until the man of God casts in the meal.

etymology: Old English dāg, kneaded paste of meal and water, cognate with the German Teig; the root sense is that which is worked or moulded — the lump between the meal-bin and the oven.
biblical_def: Dough is the kneaded lump of meal and water lying in the trough before it is baked. Scripture takes it up at two great moments. The first is the night of the Passover, when Israel went out in haste: “the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders” (Exo 12:34), and they baked unleavened cakes of it in the wilderness “because they were thrust out of Egypt, and could not tarry” (Exo 12:39). The unleavened cake is thus not merely a memorial of speed but of a redemption that would not wait upon Egypt’s convenience, and the leaven left behind stands for the corruption of the old life which the redeemed do not carry out with them. The second is the law of the firstfruits: “Ye shall offer up a cake of the first of your dough for an heave offering” (Num 15:20), and this in every generation (Num 15:21). The first of the lump was heaved to the LORD before any of it came to the family table. Paul builds doctrine on that statute: “For if the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy” (Rom 11:16) — the consecration of the first sanctifies the whole. And he presses the negative side too, twice: “a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump” (1Co 5:6; Gal 5:9). Dough is therefore a doctrine of wholes: what is put in at the kneading works through everything.
webster_summary: Paste of meal or flour moistened and kneaded, but not yet baked; in the law, the first of the dough was heaved to the LORD.
webster_full: DOUGH, paste of bread; a mass composed of flour or meal moistened and kneaded, but not baked.
Old English dāg; German Teig; that which is kneaded or worked.
The dough taken out of Egypt before it was leavened (Exo 12:34).
A cake of the first of the dough was an heave offering unto the LORD (Num 15:20-21).
Figuratively, the lump: a little leaven leaveneth the whole (1Co 5:6).
scriptures: And the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders.

And they baked unleavened cakes of the dough which they brought forth out of Egypt, for it was not leavened; because they were thrust out of Egypt, and could not tarry, neither had they prepared for themselves any victual.
Ye shall offer up a cake of the first of your dough for an heave offering: as ye do the heave offering of the threshingfloor, so shall ye heave it.
Of the first of your dough ye shall give unto the LORD an heave offering in your generations.
corruption_summary: The first of the dough has become the last of the dough — God offered what is left after everything else is spent, which reverses the whole logic of firstfruits.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse is a matter of order, not of amount. The statute does not say some of your dough; it says the first of your dough, heaved before the household ate a crumb. The modern practice inverts it: the mortgage, the instalments, the subscriptions, the holiday, and then whatever survives the month goes into the plate — and the same inversion governs the week, where the Lord gets the hours no employer wanted, and the family, where God gets whatever attention is left after the screens. This is not stinginess merely; it is a confession about who is God. The first of the lump was heaved precisely because it declared that the whole lump came from His hand and belonged to Him already. Nehemiah’s reformed remnant knew it and bound themselves to bring the firstfruits of their dough to the priests (Neh 10:37). Jeremiah shows the other end of the ruin: women kneading their dough to make cakes to the queen of heaven (Jer 7:18) — the same domestic lump, the same kitchen, offered to an idol. Dough is never neutral. It goes to somebody.

Recover the two lessons the lump was made to teach. First, holiness runs from the firstfruit through the whole: if the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy (Rom 11:16). What is consecrated at the beginning sanctifies what follows — the first hour of the day, the first day of the week, the first portion of the increase, the covenant head of the household. Second, corruption runs the same way and needs no help: a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump (1Co 5:6), so that the sin tolerated in the corner of a church or a conscience will not stay in the corner. Hence the apostle’s charge to purge out the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened, for even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us (1Co 5:7). Israel’s dough was snatched from the trough unleavened because redemption came suddenly and would not be delayed; the church keeps the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth for the same reason.
roots_summary: The kneaded lump before baking; unleavened in the Exodus haste, and its firstfruit heaved to the LORD.
roots_lines: Dough — Old English dāg, kneaded paste; German Teig.
Hebrew batseq, dough (Exo 12:34,39); 'arisah, the coarse meal or lump (Num 15:20).
Greek phurama, the lump — Rom 11:16; 1Co 5:6-7; Gal 5:9.
The Exodus dough went out unleavened because Israel could not tarry.
The first cake of the dough was an heave offering in all generations.
usage: The first of the dough, not the last — firstfruits is a question of order before it is a question of sum.
Unleavened by haste: redemption did not wait for Egypt’s bread to rise.
A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump — corruption needs no assistance to spread.

etymology: Old English ofen, cognate with the German Ofen and Latin-related forms for a baking vessel; in Scripture usually the portable clay jar or the domed floor-hearth heated with grass, thorns, and stubble.
biblical_def: The oven of Scripture is not the iron range but a clay vessel or domed hearth, heated fiercely with grass, thorns, and dung, and then swept out for the cakes to be slapped upon its inner wall. Because it was fired with whatever the field yielded, our Lord could reason from it: “if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?” (Mat 6:30). The oven appears in the law of the offerings, where the meat offering baken in the oven is the portion passed through the fire (Lev 2:4), and in the law of cleanness, where an oven touched by a carcase must be broken down (Lev 11:35). But its great use is as the standing figure of the wrath of God. “Thou shalt make them as a fiery oven in the time of thine anger” (Psa 21:9); and Malachi closes the Old Testament with it: “the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble” (Mal 4:1). Hosea turns the same image inward upon the heart: the conspirators of Israel “have made ready their heart like an oven,” banked overnight and bursting into flame in the morning (Hos 7:6). The oven is thus the whole compass of the word — the fire that bakes the offering, the fire that consumes the stubble, and the fire that smoulders in a man’s own bosom until it breaks out.
webster_summary: A place built of clay or stone, arched over and heated for baking; in Scripture a standing figure of the wrath of God and of the smouldering heart.
webster_full: OVEN, an arched cavity or place built of stone or brick, and heated for baking bread or other victuals.
Old English ofen; German Ofen. In the East, a portable clay jar or a domed floor-hearth.
Heated with grass, thorns, and stubble — whence the Lord’s argument from the grass (Mat 6:30).
The meat offering baken in the oven (Lev 2:4); an oven defiled must be broken down (Lev 11:35).
Figuratively, the day of the LORD burning as an oven (Mal 4:1; Psa 21:9).
scriptures: Mal 4:1

For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
Psa 21:9
Thou shalt make them as a fiery oven in the time of thine anger: the LORD shall swallow them up in his wrath, and the fire shall devour them.
Mat 6:30
Wherefore, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?
Hos 7:6
For they have made ready their heart like an oven, whiles they lie in wait: their baker sleepeth all the night; in the morning it burneth as a flaming fire.
corruption_summary: Malachi’s oven is seized by annihilationism as proof that the wicked are simply burned out of existence — a reading the figure will not carry and the Lord Himself forbids.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is exegetical and it is popular: because the proud are called stubble and the day burns as an oven leaving neither root nor branch, the conclusion is drawn that the punishment of the lost is extinction — a swift consuming and then nothing. Edward Fudge’s conditionalism and the annihilationism now common in broad evangelicalism rest heavily on such fuel-and-fire language. But a figure must be read by the plain teaching it illustrates, not made to overthrow it. The same Lord who spoke of the oven spoke of the fire that is not quenched and the worm that dieth not (Mar 9:44), of everlasting punishment set in the very same sentence and the very same word as life eternal (Mat 25:46), and of the smoke of their torment ascending up for ever and ever, having no rest day nor night (Rev 14:11). Stubble language describes the helplessness of the wicked before the fire, not the duration of their suffering; and the eternity of the punishment follows necessarily from the infinite worth of the God against whom the offence is committed. To read the oven as extinction is to comfort the impenitent with a sentence God never passed.

Recover what the oven is actually for. It burns two ways in Scripture, and the difference is everything. In Lev 2:4 the fire receives the offering — fine flour, mingled with oil, unleavened, passed through the heat and accepted; and that oven is a shadow of Christ, who went into the fire of the Father’s wrath in the room of His people and came out the acceptable offering. In Mal 4:1 the fire receives the stubble. Every soul stands in one relation or the other, and there is no third. Then observe the tenderness of Mat 6:30, where the very same oven becomes an argument for peace: God arrays the grass gorgeously though it is fuel by tomorrow — how much more will He clothe the children He has bought? And Hosea’s word searches the professor: a heart made ready like an oven, banked all night while the baker sleeps, bursting out in the morning. Sin does not need tending to grow hot. Let a man ask what his own heart has been smouldering over while he slept.
roots_summary: The clay baking-jar or hearth of the East; the standing emblem of the day of the LORD, and of the offering passed through fire.
roots_lines: Oven — Old English ofen; German Ofen, a baking vessel.
Hebrew tannur, the portable clay oven (Lev 2:4; Hos 7:4; Mal 4:1).
Greek klibanos, the earthen baking-jar (Mat 6:30; Luk 12:28).
Fuelled with grass, thorns, and stubble — the ground of the Lord’s argument for providence.
Two ovens in Scripture: the one that bakes the offering, the one that burns the stubble.
usage: The day that shall burn as an oven leaves the proud neither root nor branch.
The grass that fuels tomorrow’s oven is clothed today — how much more shall He clothe you?
A heart made ready like an oven burns in the morning; sin smoulders while the baker sleeps.

etymology: The old strong past participle of bake, from the Old English bacan; retained by the Authorized Version where modern English has flattened it to baked — a word almost wholly given, in Scripture, to the offerings.
biblical_def: Baken is the Authorized Version’s old participle of bake, and it belongs chiefly to the altar. The meat offering — the bloodless offering of fine flour, oil, and frankincense — might be brought raw, or parched, or dressed in the pan or the fryingpan, or it might be “baken in the oven” (Lev 2:4), and then it was to be unleavened cakes of fine flour mingled with oil, or unleavened wafers anointed with oil. The rule is absolute: “It shall not be baken with leaven” (Lev 6:17), for it is most holy. Only at Pentecost does the law command the opposite — two wave loaves “baken with leaven” (Lev 23:17), the firstfruits of a harvest of sinners gathered into one church, still carrying what corruption remains in them and accepted only because the sacrifices are offered with them. The typology of the baken offering is plain. Fine flour is ground small and evenly, without a coarse grain in the whole measure; the oil is the anointing of the Spirit; the absence of leaven is the sinlessness of the offering; and the oven is the hidden fire, for a cake baken in the oven is baked out of sight, where no eye follows it. So was the humanity of Christ perfect and even-grained, anointed without measure, unleavened by any sin, and put into a fire whose worst heat no witness saw. There is one tender domestic use besides: the angel touched the exhausted Elijah, and “there was a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head” (1Ki 19:6).
webster_summary: The old past participle of bake; used in the Authorized Version chiefly of the meat offering baken in the oven, and never with leaven.
webster_full: BAKEN, the old participle passive of bake; dried, hardened, or dressed by heat in an oven or upon coals.
Old English bacan, whence bake, baker, batch.
The meat offering baken in the oven, of fine flour mingled with oil, unleavened (Lev 2:4).
It shall not be baken with leaven; it is most holy (Lev 6:17).
Excepted: the two Pentecost wave loaves, baken with leaven (Lev 23:17).
scriptures: Lev 2:4
And if thou bring an oblation of a meat offering baken in the oven, it shall be unleavened cakes of fine flour mingled with oil, or unleavened wafers anointed with oil.
Lev 6:17
It shall not be baken with leaven. I have given it unto them for their portion of my offerings made by fire; it is most holy, as is the sin offering, and as the trespass offering.
Ye shall bring out of your habitations two wave loaves of two tenth deals: they shall be of fine flour; they shall be baken with leaven; they are the firstfruits unto the LORD.
And he looked, and, behold, there was a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head. And he did eat and drink, and laid him down again.
corruption_summary: No modern movement has redefined this old participle; the loss is that the baken offering is read as ritual detail rather than as a portrait of Christ under fire.
corruption_paragraphs: The neglect worth naming is not a redefinition but a habit of skipping. Leviticus 2 is where many a reading plan quietly dies, its ovens and pans and fryingpans dismissed as antique catering. Yet the Holy Ghost thought the manner of baking worth legislating, and the difference between the oven, the pan, and the fryingpan is the difference between a suffering wholly hidden, a suffering partly seen, and a suffering openly exposed — three views of one Christ, whose inward agony in Gethsemane and under the three hours’ darkness no eye beheld, while His outward affliction was seen of all. Fine flour speaks of a humanity with no unevenness, no knot, no coarse grain; leaven excluded speaks of a nature untouched by sin; oil mingled through the flour and poured upon it speaks of the Spirit’s anointing from the womb and at the Jordan; frankincense wholly burned speaks of a fragrance ascending to the Father which no man ever tasted. Read that way, the chapter is not tedious but adoring.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the ceremonial law is Christian doctrine in shadow, and that the shadows were drawn with deliberate exactness because the Body was exact. Nothing in the meat offering is accidental. Note too the single exception, for it guards against over-reading: at Pentecost the two wave loaves were baken with leaven (Lev 23:17), because there the offering is not Christ but the church — Jew and Gentile, two loaves and one feast, the firstfruits of the Spirit’s harvest, and leaven is in them still. They were never burned upon the altar; they were waved before the LORD, and accepted with the burnt offering and the sin offering that accompanied them. That is the gospel in a baking ordinance: the sinless One goes into the fire, and the leavened loaves are received for His sake. Finally, keep the cake baken on the coals for the fainting prophet under the juniper. The God who ordered the offerings also feeds His exhausted servants, and does not rebuke them first.
roots_summary: The Authorized Version’s participle of bake; the offering passed through hidden fire, unleavened save at Pentecost.
roots_lines: Baken — old strong past participle of bake, Old English bacan.
Hebrew 'aphah, to bake; whence 'opheh, a baker.
Baken in the oven = hidden fire; in the pan and fryingpan = suffering more openly seen.
Unleavened and mingled with oil: sinless humanity anointed by the Spirit.
The one leavened exception is Pentecost’s two wave loaves — the church, not the Christ.
usage: Baken in the oven: the fire that no witness saw, which is Gethsemane and the darkness.
It shall not be baken with leaven — the offering must be as sinless as the Offerer.
Pentecost’s loaves are baken WITH leaven, for they are the church and not the Christ.

etymology: From the Old French savouré, well-tasted, through Latin sapor, taste or relish; hence pleasing to the palate. In Scripture the word is nearly confined to one dark chapter of a father’s appetite.
biblical_def: Savoury means well-relished, pleasing to the taste, and in the Authorized Version it belongs almost entirely to Genesis 27, where it appears six times and governs the whole scene. Isaac, old and dim of eye, calls Esau and says, “make me savoury meat, such as I love, and bring it to me, that I may eat; that my soul may bless thee before I die” (Gen 27:4). Rebekah overhears, sends Jacob to the flock for two kids, and makes savoury meat “such as his father loved” (Gen 27:14); she puts the dish and the bread into Jacob’s hand (Gen 27:17), dresses him in Esau’s raiment and the skins of the kids, and the blessing is obtained by a lie repeated three times. Then Esau comes in with his own savoury meat, and Isaac trembles very exceedingly (Gen 27:31,33). Every actor in the chapter is at fault. Isaac is moving to bless the son God had said would serve the younger (Gen 25:23), and he is moved to it by his palate — the venison he loved (Gen 25:28) had long since become the hinge of his affections. Rebekah, holding a true word of God, resorts to a lie to accomplish it. Jacob takes his father’s Name in vain: “the LORD thy God brought it to me.” And yet God’s purpose according to election stands, not of works, but of Him that calleth (Rom 9:11-13) — accomplished through the sin of men, never by it, and every party paid for the deceit in years of exile, fear, and grief.
webster_summary: Pleasing to the taste; well-relished. Used in Scripture almost wholly of the dish by which Isaac was to bless, and by which he was deceived.
webster_full: SAVOURY, pleasing to the taste; palatable; that gratifies the appetite or relish.
From Old French savouré, from Latin sapor, taste, relish.
Isaac’s charge: make me savoury meat, such as I love (Gen 27:4).
Rebekah made savoury meat such as his father loved, of two kids of the goats (Gen 27:9,14).
Esau also made savoury meat, and came too late (Gen 27:31).
scriptures: Gen 27:4
And make me savoury meat, such as I love, and bring it to me, that I may eat; that my soul may bless thee before I die.
And he went, and fetched, and brought them to his mother: and his mother made savoury meat, such as his father loved.
And she gave the savoury meat and the bread, which she had prepared, into the hand of her son Jacob.
And he also had made savoury meat, and brought it unto his father, and said unto his father, Let my father arise, and eat of his son's venison, that thy soul may bless me.
corruption_summary: Genesis 27 is preached as though Rebekah and Jacob were God’s clever instruments, their lying sanctified by the outcome — the oldest excuse in the world dressed as providence.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is a doctrine of ends and means smuggled into the pulpit. Because the blessing did in fact fall where God had said it would, the lie that fetched it gets quietly commended: Rebekah becomes shrewd, Jacob becomes enterprising, and the savoury meat becomes a sanctified stratagem. Scripture never says so. It records the deceit without a syllable of approval and then lets the reader watch the bill come due — Jacob flees the house and does not see his mother’s face again; he is deceived in his turn by Laban with the elder-for-the-younger trick, deceived again by his own sons with a kid’s blood on a coat, and mourns twenty years for a son who is alive. God’s decree is not a licence, and His overruling of sin is not His approval of it. The Confession is exact here: the almighty power, unsearchable wisdom, and infinite goodness of God so extend themselves to the first fall and all other sins that His providence ordereth them to His own holy ends, yet so as the sinfulness proceedeth only from the creature, and not from God (LBCF 5.4). Say plainly what the chapter says: election is God’s, and the fraud was man’s.

The second lesson is Isaac’s, and it is the one that goes unpreached. A blessing of covenantal weight, involving the line of Messiah, is set on the far side of a plate of game — because the patriarch had let his palate govern him for decades. It began small and domestic: Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of his venison (Gen 25:28). That is how appetite becomes a ruler. It buys a father’s partiality first, then his judgment, then his obedience to a plain word from God about which son should serve which. And the Scripture is full of the same figure: whose god is their belly (Php 3:19), the drowsy man clothed with rags (Pro 23:21), a people who sat down to eat and rose up to play. Modern life has raised the palate into an identity, with food as ritual, restaurant as pilgrimage, and diet as moral standing. Recover the plain Reformed rule instead: eat and drink to the glory of God (1Co 10:31), and never let a dish govern a decision that belongs to the Lord.
roots_summary: Well-tasted, palatable; the word of Genesis 27, where a father’s appetite and a family’s deceit met God’s unbreakable election.
roots_lines: Savoury — Old French savouré, from Latin sapor, taste, relish.
Hebrew mat'am, a dainty or well-relished dish, from ta'am, to taste (Gen 27:4).
The word occurs six times, all in Genesis 27, and once as the dish Esau brought too late.
The dish was the hinge: Isaac loved Esau because he did eat of his venison (Gen 25:28).
The blessing stood because election stood — not of works, but of Him that calleth.
usage: Isaac’s palate had been governing him since Gen 25:28; Gen 27 is only the bill.
The savoury meat was a lie’s vehicle — God overruled the deceit, He did not approve it.
Jacob who deceived with a kid’s skin was deceived at last with a kid’s blood.

etymology: From the Old French morsel, a little bite, diminutive of mors, a bite, from Latin mordere, to bite; hence the smallest portion of food that can be handed to a man — and in Scripture, the measure of both hospitality and folly.
biblical_def: A morsel is a bite, a mouthful, the least portion of bread one man can offer another — and Scripture uses that smallness in three directions. First, as the modest word of hospitality. Abraham runs from his tent door to three strangers and says, “I will fetch a morsel of bread, and comfort ye your hearts” (Gen 18:5), and then sets before them a calf tender and good, with butter, milk, and three measures of fine meal — the promise small, the table large, which is the manner of true hospitality; and he entertained the Angel of the LORD unawares (Heb 13:2). Boaz says to the foreign widow gleaning in his field, “dip thy morsel in the vinegar” (Rut 2:14), and she ate and was sufficed and left some over. Second, as the measure of a quiet house against a quarrelsome one: “Better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife” (Pro 17:1). Third, and terribly, as the price of a birthright: Esau, says the Holy Ghost, was a profane person, “who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright” (Heb 12:16). The word appears once more in the upper room, where the Lord dipped the sop and gave it to Judas Iscariot, and after the sop Satan entered into him (Joh 13:26-27) — the last morsel of covenant kindness offered to a traitor’s hand.
webster_summary: A bite; a mouthful; a small piece of food. In Scripture the token of hospitality, the measure of a peaceable house, and the price Esau took.
webster_full: MORSEL, a bite; a mouthful; a small piece of food; hence a small quantity of anything.
Old French morsel, diminutive of mors, a bite; Latin mordere, to bite.
Abraham’s morsel of bread to the three strangers (Gen 18:5).
Boaz to Ruth: dip thy morsel in the vinegar (Rut 2:14).
Better a dry morsel with quietness than a house of feasting with strife (Pro 17:1).
scriptures: Gen 18:5
And I will fetch a morsel of bread, and comfort ye your hearts; after that ye shall pass on: for therefore are ye come to your servant. And they said, So do, as thou hast said.
Rut 2:14

And Boaz said unto her, At mealtime come thou hither, and eat of the bread, and dip thy morsel in the vinegar. And she sat beside the reapers: and he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left.
Pro 17:1
Better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife.
Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.
corruption_summary: Hospitality has been outsourced to the restaurant and the church programme, and the morsel that once opened a home has been swallowed by a culture that makes eating an identity.
corruption_paragraphs: Two live misuses meet in this small word. The first is the death of household hospitality. Abraham’s morsel was fetched from his own tent by his own running feet; Boaz handed his own parched corn to a woman who had no claim on him; and the New Testament requires the same of every Christian house — given to hospitality (Rom 12:13), and of an elder, a lover of hospitality (Tit 1:8), and of all, use hospitality one to another without grudging (1Pe 4:9). What has replaced it is either the restaurant, where money buys company without covenant, or the church programme, where hospitality is delegated to a committee and a rota. Neither opens a door. The reason usually given is that the house is not fit to be seen, which turns hospitality into performance and then abolishes it; Scripture asked only for a morsel and a welcome. The second misuse is the elevation of the appetite: eating raised into a personality, the table made a stage, the meal made a moral statement. Pro 17:1 answers it in one line — a dry morsel with quietness is better than an house full of sacrifices with strife.

Recover the morsel at both ends, for the same word measures the highest kindness and the lowest bargain. At the highest: a bite of bread offered in the name of Christ is never small. He that receiveth you receiveth me, and a cup of cold water only, given to a disciple, shall in no wise lose its reward (Mat 10:40-42). Abraham did not know what he was entertaining, and neither do we. At the lowest: one morsel of meat is the recorded price of the birthright, and Hebrews sets it as a warning to a church, not to a pagan — look diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God, lest there be any profane person as Esau. And the darkest morsel of all was handed by the Lord Himself. He dipped the sop and gave it to Judas, an act of honour at an eastern table, the last kindness a traitor would ever receive from those hands; and Judas took the bread and went immediately out, and it was night. A morsel can be the beginning of communion or the last stroke of hardening. It is never neutral.
roots_summary: A bite of bread; the token of hospitality, the measure of a quiet house, and the price of a birthright.
roots_lines: Morsel — Old French mors, a bite, from Latin mordere, to bite.
Hebrew path, a fragment or bit of bread (Gen 18:5; Rut 2:14; Pro 17:1).
Greek brosis, a thing eaten — one morsel of meat (Heb 12:16).
Promise small, table large: Abraham offers a morsel and sets on a calf and fine meal.
The sop in the upper room was a morsel of honour given to a traitor (Joh 13:26).
usage: Abraham promises a morsel and serves a feast — hospitality understates and overgives.
Better a dry morsel with quietness than an house full of sacrifices with strife.
One morsel of meat is the whole recorded price of a birthright.

etymology: From the Old French bouteillier, the bottle-bearer, from bouteille, a bottle; hence the officer who has charge of the wine and presents the cup — in Egypt and Persia a post of great trust, since the king’s life passed through his hands.
biblical_def: The butler is the cupbearer, the officer who tasted and presented the king’s wine — a post held only by a man the king trusted with his life, and therefore a position near the throne. Pharaoh’s chief butler and chief baker both offended their lord and were put into the ward of the captain of the guard, into the very prison where Joseph was bound (Gen 40:1-3). One night each dreamed, and in the morning they were sad, and Joseph asked them why, and said, “Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you” (Gen 40:8). The butler saw a vine with three branches budding, blossoming, and ripening into clusters which he pressed into Pharaoh’s cup; Joseph read it: within three days he would be restored (Gen 40:13). And so it fell out on Pharaoh’s birthday: the butler was restored to his butlership and gave the cup into Pharaoh’s hand (Gen 40:21). Joseph had asked one thing — think on me when it shall be well with thee — and the chapter closes with the flattest sentence in Genesis: “Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him” (Gen 40:23). Two full years passed (Gen 41:1). Then Pharaoh dreamed, the magicians failed, and the butler said, “I do remember my faults this day” (Gen 41:9) — and Joseph was shaved and brought out to stand before Pharaoh at the exact hour that saved two nations from famine.
webster_summary: A cupbearer; the servant who has charge of the wine and presents the cup to his lord. Pharaoh’s butler was restored, and forgat the man who read his dream.
webster_full: BUTLER, a servant or officer in a great family, who has the care of the liquors and plate, and presents the cup.
Old French bouteillier, from bouteille, a bottle; the bottle-bearer.
In the courts of Egypt and Persia a place of high trust, being near the king’s person.
Pharaoh’s chief butler dreamed of the vine, and was restored to his butlership (Gen 40:9-21).
He forgat Joseph two full years, and remembered him at the appointed hour (Gen 40:23; 41:9).
scriptures: Gen 40:1
And it came to pass after these things, that the butler of the king of Egypt and his baker had offended their lord the king of Egypt.
Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thine head, and restore thee unto thy place: and thou shalt deliver Pharaoh's cup into his hand, after the former manner when thou wast his butler.
And he restored the chief butler unto his butlership again; and he gave the cup into Pharaoh's hand:
Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.
corruption_summary: Joseph’s prison is retold as a motivational parable — keep believing and your dream will come true — when the text is about a God who governs the memory of a forgetful servant.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse is the motivational hijacking of Genesis 39–41. Joseph is made the hero of perseverance, the prison is made a season of personal growth, and the moral is that your dream will come to pass if you keep your attitude right. Every part of that is out of joint with the text. Joseph is not waiting on a dream of his own; he is interpreting other men’s, and telling them plainly that interpretations belong to God. He does not rise by attitude; he rises because a butler’s memory failed for exactly two years and then recovered at exactly the moment Pharaoh dreamed. And the account’s own summary is not a maxim about believing in yourself but a doctrine of God: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive (Gen 50:20). Prosperity preaching needs the story to be about Joseph. Scripture insists that it is about the LORD, who was with him in the pit, in Potiphar’s house, and in the prison, and who had the famine, the granaries, and the survival of the covenant family in view the whole time.

Recover the doctrine of providence at the point where it is hardest to feel — the delay. Joseph asked the butler for one favour, and got nothing for seven hundred days. It looked like the last door closing. In fact the forgetting was as much God’s work as the remembering, for had the butler spoken in the first week, Joseph would have been released as a favour to a foreign slave and vanished. He was kept in irons until the hour when the throne itself needed him, and then he went from the dungeon to the second chariot in a single day. That is not coincidence retrofitted with piety; it is the ordinary manner of God’s government, who upholdeth, directeth, disposeth, and governeth all creatures and things, from the greatest even to the least, by His most wise and holy providence (LBCF 5.1). The believer whose case has been forgotten by every man who promised to speak for him should mark the two years and the two dreams, and remember that the delay had a calendar.
roots_summary: The king’s cupbearer; restored on the third day, and forgetful two years, that God’s hour might be kept exactly.
roots_lines: Butler — Old French bouteillier, the bottle-bearer; the cupbearer of a great house.
Hebrew mashqeh, one who gives drink, a cupbearer (Gen 40:1; cf. Neh 1:11 of Nehemiah).
The vine with three branches: three days to restoration (Gen 40:12-13).
The one favour Joseph asked was forgotten for two full years (Gen 40:23; 41:1).
“I do remember my faults this day” — the memory returned on God’s schedule (Gen 41:9).
usage: The butler’s forgetting was as providential as his remembering — the delay had a calendar.
Do not interpretations belong to God? Joseph disowns the gift before he uses it.
A cupbearer’s trust was his master’s life; hence his nearness to the throne.

etymology: Old English bæcere, from bacan, to bake; the tradesman who kneads and fires the bread. Jerusalem had a bakers’ street (Jer 37:21), and Pharaoh a chief baker who went out of prison to a tree.
biblical_def: The baker is the tradesman of the oven, and Scripture gives him three appearances of very different weight. He is an ordinary craft: Jerusalem had a bakers’ street, from which Jeremiah in the court of the prison was given his daily piece of bread until all the bread in the city was spent (Jer 37:21). He is a figure of the fevered heart: Israel’s adulterous conspirators are “as an oven heated by the baker,” whose fire needs no stirring while he sleeps, and burns as a flaming fire in the morning (Hos 7:4,6). But the baker of Scripture is chiefly Pharaoh’s. He and the chief butler offended their lord together, were imprisoned together, dreamed on the same night, and heard their interpretations from the same mouth. The butler saw a budding vine and a cup; the baker saw three white baskets on his head, the uppermost full of bakemeats for Pharaoh, and the birds eating out of it. Joseph gave him the truth without softening it: “Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thy head from off thee, and shall hang thee on a tree; and the birds shall eat thy flesh from off thee” (Gen 40:19). And it came to pass exactly so: Pharaoh lifted up the head of both — the one to his office, the other to a gallows (Gen 40:20-22). Two men, one offence, one prison, one night, one interpreter, one word about the lifting up of a head, and two eternally different ends.
webster_summary: One whose occupation is to bake bread. Pharaoh’s chief baker was hanged on the third day, while his fellow prisoner was restored.
webster_full: BAKER, one whose occupation is to bake bread, biscuit, or the like.
Old English bæcere, from bacan, to bake; whence also batch and bakehouse.
Jerusalem had a bakers’ street, whence Jeremiah was fed in the siege (Jer 37:21).
Pharaoh’s chief baker dreamed of three white baskets and the birds (Gen 40:16-17).
Hosea’s figure: a heart like an oven heated by the baker, that burns while he sleeps (Hos 7:4,6).
scriptures: Gen 40:2
And Pharaoh was wroth against two of his officers, against the chief of the butlers, and against the chief of the bakers.
When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was good, he said unto Joseph, I also was in my dream, and, behold, I had three white baskets on my head:
Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thy head from off thee, and shall hang thee on a tree; and the birds shall eat thy flesh from off thee.
But he hanged the chief baker: as Joseph had interpreted to them.
corruption_summary: The two prisoners are one of Scripture’s sharpest pictures of election and reprobation — and it is precisely the doctrine modern preaching most wants to deny.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 40 offends the modern ear because it destroys the assumption that God’s dealings must be even-handed in the way men measure evenness. Two officers, equally guilty, equally imprisoned, equally dreaming, hear equally from the same prophet; and one goes back to the cup while the other goes to the tree. Nothing in the narrative makes the butler the better man — his one recorded act afterward is to forget his benefactor for two years. The distinction is not in them. It is the same distinction Paul presses from another pair of brothers in the same book: the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth (Rom 9:11). The Arminian scheme must locate the difference in the creature, and so makes election a response to foreseen faith; universalism abolishes the difference altogether; and much popular evangelicalism simply declines to mention reprobation and hopes no one reads the chapter. But Scripture states both sides plainly: vessels of mercy afore prepared unto glory, and vessels of wrath fitted to destruction (Rom 9:22-23); some men and angels predestinated unto everlasting life, and others foreordained to everlasting death (LBCF 3.3).

Guard the doctrine from the two errors that always crowd it. First, God is not the author of sin, and reprobation does no violence to the will of the creature: the chief baker was hanged for his own offence against his own lord, justly, and Pharaoh needed no divine compulsion to be wroth. The decree of reprobation passes by, and appoints to dishonour for sin — it does not make men sinners. Second, the doctrine is not for speculation but for adoration and for preaching. Joseph told the baker the truth. He did not flatter a condemned man with a comfortable interpretation, and he did not withhold the interpretation because it was hard. Ministers who will not preach a real judgment because it makes hearers uneasy have decided to be kinder than God, and they are not. And for those who are in Christ, the whole weight of the chapter falls the other way: if the difference had lain in you, you would have gone to the tree. The lifting up of the head is the same phrase for both men; grace alone determined which lifting was which.
roots_summary: The tradesman of the oven; Pharaoh’s chief baker, one of two prisoners whose one night ended in two destinies.
roots_lines: Baker — Old English bæcere, from bacan, to bake.
Hebrew 'opheh, a baker, participle of 'aphah, to bake (Gen 40:1; Hos 7:4).
Three white baskets = three days, as the vine’s three branches were three days.
“Lift up thy head” is used of both men — to a cup, and to a gallows (Gen 40:13,19).
Jerusalem’s bakers’ street fed Jeremiah till the bread of the city was spent (Jer 37:21).
usage: One prison, one night, one interpreter, two destinies — and the difference was not in the men.
Joseph gave the condemned man the true interpretation, unsoftened.
Hosea’s baker sleeps while the oven heats: sin needs no tending to burn.

etymology: From honey and comb, the waxen cells wrought by bees; hence honey still in its comb, unstrained — the sweetest form of the sweetest thing the ancient table knew.
biblical_def: The honeycomb is honey still in the wax, taken from the rock or the wild wood and eaten unstrained — and Scripture always means by it something sweeter than sweet. The Psalmist ranks the judgments of the LORD above gold, “sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb” (Psa 19:10), so that the comb becomes the measure by which the word of God exceeds every earthly pleasure. Proverbs applies it to speech: “Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones” (Pro 16:24), and warns that the lips of a strange woman also drop as an honeycomb while her end is bitter as wormwood (Pro 5:3-4) — sweetness is no proof of safety. The full soul loatheth an honeycomb, but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet (Pro 27:7), which is the whole doctrine of spiritual appetite in one line. In the Song, the Bridegroom says, “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey” (Son 5:1), and the bride’s lips drop as the honeycomb (Son 4:11). But the greatest occurrence is the plainest. On the evening of the resurrection, when the disciples believed not for joy and wondered, the risen Christ asked, “Have ye here any meat?” and they gave Him a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb, “and he took it, and did eat before them” (Luk 24:42-43). A spirit hath not flesh and bones. The honeycomb is evidence.
webster_summary: The waxen cells wrought by bees, filled with honey; in Scripture the measure of the word’s sweetness, and part of the risen Christ’s supper.
webster_full: HONEYCOMB, the waxen structure of cells formed by bees for the reception of honey.
From honey and comb; honey in the comb, unstrained.
The judgments of the LORD are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Psa 19:10).
Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones (Pro 16:24).
The risen Lord ate of a broiled fish and of an honeycomb before His disciples (Luk 24:42-43).
scriptures: More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb.
Pro 27:7
The full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet.
Son 5:1

I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse: I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk: eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved.
And he took it, and did eat before them.
corruption_summary: The honeycomb of Luke 24 is quietly set aside wherever the resurrection is reduced to a spiritual impression in the disciples’ hearts rather than a body raised.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is ancient and modern at once. The ancient form was docetism and the Gnostic denial that Christ had a true body at all; the modern form is the liberal-Protestant reduction of the resurrection to a symbol — Bultmann’s dictum that Jesus rose into the kerygma, Schleiermacher’s inward Christ, and the popular pulpit version in which Easter means that love survives death or that hope always returns in spring. Luke closes that door with a piece of fish and a piece of honeycomb. The Lord did not merely appear; He asked for food, took it, and ate it before them, having first said, Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have (Luk 24:39). Eating is the one thing an apparition cannot do. The honeycomb is therefore not a domestic detail but an apologetic: the same body that was crucified, glorified and no longer subject to death, was in that room and consumed ordinary food. Deny it and the whole gospel falls, for if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain, ye are yet in your sins (1Co 15:17).

Recover both edges of the comb. Toward Christ: the risen body is the pledge of ours, for He shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body (Php 3:21), and the believer’s hope is not a disembodied survival but a resurrection of this flesh. Toward the word: Psa 19:10 sets the honeycomb as the standard the Scriptures exceed, and the test is experimental. Pro 27:7 explains why so many find the Bible dull — the full soul loatheth an honeycomb. It is not that the comb has lost its sweetness; it is that the soul is stuffed with other food. Ezekiel ate the roll and it was in his mouth as honey for sweetness (Eze 3:3), and John did the same and found it bitter in the belly (Rev 10:10), for the word that delights also digests hard. And take the warning of Pro 5:3: the strange woman’s lips drop as an honeycomb too. Sweetness is not the test of truth; Scripture is.
roots_summary: Honey in the wax, unstrained; the measure of the word’s sweetness and a proof of the risen Lord’s true body.
roots_lines: Honeycomb — honey + comb; the waxen cells with the honey still in them.
Hebrew nopheth, the dropping comb (Psa 19:10; Pro 5:3; Pro 24:13).
Greek melission kerion, a comb of honey (Luk 24:42).
The comb exceeds strained honey as the word exceeds much fine gold.
Luk 24:42-43 is evidence, not decoration: a spirit hath not flesh and bones.
usage: Sweeter than honey and the honeycomb — the word’s worth measured against the sweetest thing known.
The full soul loatheth an honeycomb: a dull Bible usually means a stuffed heart.
He took it, and did eat before them — the honeycomb proves a real body raised.

etymology: From the Old French caudron, through Latin caldarium, a hot bath or boiling vessel, from calidus, hot; hence a great pot for seething flesh — a temple vessel, and a prophet’s figure for a city under judgment.
biblical_def: A caldron is a great boiling pot for seething flesh. It was a vessel of the sanctuary — the fleshhook was struck into “the pan, or kettle, or caldron, or pot” at Shiloh (1Sa 2:14), the caldrons of brass were carried away by the Chaldeans when the temple was stripped (Jer 52:18), and Josiah’s passover offerings were sod in pots and caldrons and pans (2Ch 35:13). But the word’s doctrinal weight is in Ezekiel. The princes of Jerusalem, secure behind their walls after the first deportation, had a proverb: “It is not near; let us build houses: this city is the caldron, and we be the flesh” (Eze 11:3). Their meaning was comfortable — the walls are the iron pot, we are the choice meat inside, protected; judgment falls on the exiles outside, not on us. The LORD takes their own figure and turns it against them. Yes, He says, there is flesh in this caldron: “Your slain whom ye have laid in the midst of it, they are the flesh, and this city is the caldron: but I will bring you forth out of the midst of it” (Eze 11:7). The men they had murdered are the meat; the murderers will be dragged out of the pot to be judged in the border of Israel by the sword they did not fear (Eze 11:10-11). Ezekiel 24 completes it: the caldron is set on the fire with its scum still in it, and the fire is heaped until the very brass burns.
webster_summary: A large kettle or boiler for seething flesh; in Ezekiel, the false proverb of a city that thought its walls made it safe.
webster_full: CALDRON, a large kettle or boiler, of copper or other metal, for boiling flesh or other things.
Old French caudron, Latin caldarium, from calidus, hot.
A vessel of the sanctuary service (1Sa 2:14; 2Ch 35:13; Jer 52:18).
The proverb of Jerusalem: this city is the caldron, and we be the flesh (Eze 11:3).
The LORD’s answer: the slain are the flesh, and the murderers shall be brought forth (Eze 11:7,11).
scriptures: Eze 11:3
Which say, It is not near; let us build houses: this city is the caldron, and we be the flesh.
Eze 11:7
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Your slain whom ye have laid in the midst of it, they are the flesh, and this city is the caldron: but I will bring you forth out of the midst of it.
This city shall not be your caldron, neither shall ye be the flesh in the midst thereof; but I will judge you in the border of Israel:
Mic 3:3
Who also eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them; and they break their bones, and chop them in pieces, as for the pot, and as flesh within the caldron.
corruption_summary: The caldron proverb is carnal security in three clauses — it is not near, let us build houses, we are the safe ones — and it is spoken in churches still.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse is presumption, and Ezekiel gives its exact liturgy. It is not near — judgment is postponed indefinitely, the warnings belong to another generation, the prophets are alarmists. Let us build houses — therefore invest in the present order as though it were permanent. This city is the caldron, and we be the flesh — and we are the insiders, the chosen, the protected, whatever we do. That last clause is the deadly one, because it converts a covenant privilege into a charm. The Jerusalem that said it had the temple, the ark’s memory, the Davidic city, and the sacrifices, and it had murdered men in its own streets; and it reasoned that the walls would hold because God’s house stood inside them. Jeremiah met the same slogan — The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these (Jer 7:4). The church version is a baptism certificate, a family name, a membership roll, an orthodox confession recited by a heart that has never repented; and the answer is the same. Privilege that is presumed upon becomes the very ground of the sentence: You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you (Amo 3:2).

Recover what the LORD does with their figure, for it is a model of how God answers the self-secure. He does not deny the caldron. He grants it and redefines the contents. There is flesh in the pot — the men you slew; and the security you claimed will be taken from you precisely by being brought out of the walls you trusted, to be judged in the border of Israel where the sword waits. Judgment for such men is not being kept in the pot but being poured out of it. Then hear the mercy that follows in the same chapter, addressed to the despised exiles the princes had written off: Although I have cast them far off among the heathen, yet will I be to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they shall come (Eze 11:16), and I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them an heart of flesh (Eze 11:19). The men inside the walls had stone hearts and a stone city; the men outside had nothing, and were given a sanctuary and a new heart. Safety was never the masonry. It was the covenant God who makes hearts new.
roots_summary: A great seething pot; Jerusalem’s proverb of false security, turned against her by the LORD.
roots_lines: Caldron — Old French caudron, Latin caldarium, from calidus, hot.
Hebrew sir, a pot or caldron (Eze 11:3); dud, a kettle or basket (1Sa 2:14).
A sanctuary vessel before it was a prophetic figure (2Ch 35:13; Jer 52:18).
The princes’ proverb: walls as the iron pot, themselves as the protected flesh.
The LORD’s reversal: the slain are the flesh, and the secure shall be brought forth to judgment.
usage: “It is not near; let us build houses” — the three clauses of carnal security.
God grants the figure and reverses it: the flesh in the pot is the men you murdered.
To the exiles outside the walls He promised a little sanctuary and a heart of flesh.
